lessons.title: Reading your payslip: withholding is an estimate, not your tax
lessons.explanation: A payslip reports gross pay, then subtracts several kinds of items, then reports net pay. The kinds matter because they behave differently and only some of them are under your control. Statutory items are set by law: federal income tax withholding, Social Security and Medicare taxes collected under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act, and state or local income tax where those exist. Benefit items are elected: health, dental, life and disability premiums, and retirement plan contributions. Court-ordered items, such as wage garnishments, are legal obligations. Voluntary items are anything else an employer offers. The most important idea in this lesson is that income tax withholding is a payment on account, not the tax itself. The employer computes it from the Form W-4 you filed and the Internal Revenue Service's published withholding tables, which annualise your pay, apply a filing status and a bracket schedule, and divide the result back into your pay periods. Your actual liability is determined later, from your total income, filing status, deductions and credits. Withhold too little across the year and you may owe a balance plus a penalty; withhold too much and you have lent the government money interest-free until your refund arrives. Payroll taxes behave differently again: they are flat statutory rates applied to wages, they are not affected by most withholding elections, and the Social Security portion stops applying above an annual wage base while the Medicare portion does not.
lessons.example: Take a stated case: gross pay of $5,000 a month, or $60,000 a year, with no state income tax in this illustration, no benefit deductions, and a single filer claiming no adjustments. Social Security tax is 6.2% of the month, or $310.00, and Medicare tax is 1.45%, or $72.50, so the employee's payroll tax for the month is $382.50. Social Security and Medicare rates and the wage base are set by statute and published by the Service; the rate figures used here are those published in the Service's own topic page on Social Security and Medicare withholding rates, and they can be changed by legislation, so check the current page before relying on them. For federal income tax, use a simplified annualised calculation: gross of $60,000 less the published standard deduction for a single filer for tax year 2026 of $16,100 leaves $43,900 of taxable income; applying the published single brackets gives $1,240.00 at 10% on the first $12,400 and $3,780.00 at 12% on the next $31,500, for $5,020.00 a year or $418.33 a month. That is an illustration of the arithmetic of annualised withholding, not a substitute for the employer's percentage-method tables and worksheets, which are what payroll actually uses. Net pay in the illustration is $5,000.00 minus $382.50 minus $418.33, which is $4,199.17 a month, or $50,390.00 a year. Notice what the comparison shows. The average federal income tax is 8.37% of gross, the marginal rate on the next dollar of income is 12%, and the payroll tax on the next dollar is 7.65% while wages are below the Social Security wage base, which for 2026 is published as $184,500. Above that base the marginal payroll rate falls to 1.45%, plus an additional 0.9% Medicare tax once wages exceed $200,000, which employers must withhold without regard to filing status.
lessons.question: A worker's withholding turns out to be $1,200 less than the tax owed for the year. What is the correct action, and why?
lessons.answer: Update the Form W-4 so future withholding matches the expected liability, using the Service's estimator, because withholding is a payment on account and the shortfall is a timing problem
lessons.distractor: Ask payroll to withhold a larger share from the final pay periods, since employers must reconcile the year and can compute the exact liability
lessons.correction: An employer cannot know your total income, filing status, deductions or credits, so it cannot compute your liability; it applies the tables to the Form W-4 you filed. The mismatch is a withholding election problem, and the tools for fixing it are the Form W-4 and the Service's withholding estimator, which can produce a pre-filled form. Leaving it alone means owing a balance, possibly with an accuracy-related penalty, and adjusting once at the end of the year is both late and outside the employer's role.

depth.definitions: Gross pay is total compensation before deductions. Net pay is what is deposited. Withholding is tax paid on your behalf during the year against the liability that will be computed later. Payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act comprise the Social Security and Medicare portions, each shared between employee and employer at the same employee rate, with the Social Security portion limited by an annual wage base that is set by statute and published, and with an additional 0.9% Medicare tax withheld on wages above a threshold. The marginal rate applies to the next dollar; the average rate is total tax divided by income. The standard deduction is a fixed amount that reduces taxable income and is adjusted annually. A pre-tax election, such as a retirement plan deferral or a qualified benefit premium, reduces taxable income but generally does not reduce payroll taxes. A garnishment is a legal order to withhold from wages. Year-to-date columns on a payslip accumulate each item and are the primary tool for auditing the slip.
depth.mechanism: Three separate systems are running on the same paycheque, and confusing them produces most of the errors people make. The first is income tax, which is progressive and depends on your whole year, so the employer must approximate: it annualises each pay period, subtracts the standard deduction or the amounts you elected, applies the bracket schedule, and divides back down. The approximation is why the amount withheld is routinely wrong in one direction or the other, and why a pay rise, a second job, a bonus, a mid-year marriage or a new dependant changes the correct figure. The second is payroll tax, which is not progressive across the year in the same way: it is a flat percentage with a ceiling on the Social Security portion, so the marginal cost of the next dollar falls once the wage base is passed, and the cumulative amount stops rising for the base-limited portion. The third is the benefit layer, where pre-tax elections reduce income tax but not payroll tax, which is the reason a retirement deferral saves less than the deferral multiplied by the marginal rate. Two boundary conditions belong with all three. Rates, wage bases, thresholds, bracket boundaries, standard deduction amounts and credit values are statutory, are adjusted for inflation on a schedule, and can be changed by legislation; the Service publishes them annually, and the underlying figures should be read from the current year's release rather than remembered. And state and local income tax rules vary enormously, including places with no income tax at all, so a national illustration is not a withholding calculation for any particular person.
depth.secondExample: Watch the payroll-tax arithmetic change shape as income rises, using the published 2026 wage base of $184,500 and the published employee rates of 6.2% and 1.45%. At a $60,000 salary the employee pays $3,720.00 of Social Security tax and $870.00 of Medicare tax, a total of $4,590.00. At $184,500 the Social Security portion is at its maximum, $11,439.00, and Medicare is $2,675.25, totalling $14,114.25. At $200,000 the Social Security portion is unchanged at $11,439.00 while Medicare rises to $2,900.00, and the additional 0.9% has not yet begun because the threshold is exactly $200,000. At $250,000 the additional Medicare tax applies to $50,000 of wages, adding $450.00, so total payroll tax is $11,439.00 plus $3,625.00 plus $450.00, which is $15,514.00. The pattern is the point: the marginal payroll rate is 7.65% up to the base, then 1.45%, then 2.35% above the additional-Medicare threshold, while the figure everyone remembers -- 7.65% -- describes only the first band. Now add the benefit layer in the same illustration. A 6% retirement deferral on $5,000 a month is $300.00 and reduces the illustrated monthly income tax by $36.00, which is $300.00 times the 12% marginal rate, while the payroll tax of $382.50 does not change. A 10% deferral saves $60.00 of illustrated income tax a month on $500.00 deferred. Both figures are arithmetic of the stated rates, not advice about how much to defer.
depth.mistake: The most common error is reading the marginal bracket as the rate applied to all income, so a worker in the 12% bracket believes a raise will cost 12% of gross when the actual reduction is 12% plus 7.65% of payroll tax on the next dollar, or about 19.65% while below the wage base -- and much less above it. The second error is treating a refund as free money rather than as the return of an interest-free loan, which hides whether the withholding election was right. The third is assuming payroll taxes are adjustable through the Form W-4, which they are not. The fourth is comparing take-home pay between two offers without comparing gross pay, the payroll tax position and the benefit elections, which is how an offer with a higher salary and worse benefits can look better than it is. A diagnostic that catches all four: pick one payslip and verify three things -- that gross pay times the number of pay periods equals the annual figure you believe, that each deduction line matches the election you actually made, and that the year-to-date figures reconcile with your own record of the year. If the third check has never been performed, the withholding election is unverified.
depth.application: Take your most recent payslip and build a five-column table: item, amount this period, amount year to date, whether it is statutory, elected, court-ordered or voluntary, and whether it is pre-tax for income tax purposes, for payroll tax purposes, or for neither. Then compute your own effective income tax rate on gross pay and your marginal rate on the next dollar, and write one sentence stating whether your withholding election is likely to produce a balance due or a refund, with the reason. If you expect a mismatch, use the Service's withholding estimator and complete a new Form W-4 rather than asking payroll to adjust informally. Self-review rubric: the audit is complete when every deduction is classified in all three dimensions, when the gross-to-net arithmetic is shown to reconcile, and when the expected year-end position is stated as an estimate with its reason. It fails if a deduction is listed without its classification, or if a tax figure is quoted from memory rather than from the current year's published source.
depth.summary: A payslip contains three systems: income tax withholding, which is an annualised estimate of a liability that depends on your whole year; statutory payroll taxes, which are flat percentages with a wage base and additional thresholds; and benefit, court-ordered and voluntary deductions, of which the pre-tax ones reduce income tax but usually not payroll tax. Withholding is not the tax, refunds are not gifts, rates and thresholds are statutory and republished annually, and the way to fix a mismatch is a new Form W-4 supported by the Service's estimator rather than an informal request to payroll.

lessons.title: Retirement accounts as containers: the tax rule is not the investment
lessons.explanation: A retirement account is a container that determines when money is taxed. What sits inside it is a separate decision. Three container types cover most situations. A tax-deferred container, such as a traditional individual retirement arrangement or a 401(k) plan, generally lets contributions be made before tax or deducted from taxable income, allows growth without annual tax, and taxes distributions as ordinary income when they are received. A tax-free container, such as a Roth version of either, takes contributions after tax and generally allows qualified distributions without tax. A taxable brokerage account has no special treatment at all: dividends, interest and realised gains are taxed as they arise. The Service describes a 401(k) as a feature of a qualified profit-sharing plan in which elective salary deferrals are excluded from taxable income except for designated Roth deferrals, employers may contribute, and distributions including earnings are includible in taxable income at retirement except for qualified distributions of designated Roth accounts. Two questions decide most container comparisons: when is the money taxed, and at what rate? If the rate at contribution and the rate at withdrawal are the same, the tax-deferred and Roth containers produce identical after-tax results, which surprises most people. The comparison only diverges when the rates differ, and the direction of the difference is what should be stated before choosing. What a container does not do is change the investments available, the fees charged inside it, or the fact that the money has to be invested in something.
lessons.example: Compare the containers on one stream. A saver puts $7,000 a year aside for thirty years at an assumed 6% annual return compounded annually. In a tax-deferred container the balance is $553,407.30 before any withdrawal tax. If the whole balance is drawn at an assumed flat rate of 12% the after-tax result is $486,998.43; at 22% it is $431,657.70; at 32% it is $376,316.97. Now the Roth version, compared honestly on the same starting resources: if the saver's marginal rate at contribution is 22%, then $7,000 of pre-tax resources becomes $5,460 of after-tax contribution, which grows tax-free for thirty years to $431,657.70. That is exactly the tax-deferred result at a 22% withdrawal rate, which demonstrates the identity: equal rates, equal outcome. The comparison becomes a judgement only when the two rates differ. Against a withdrawal rate of 12%, the tax-deferred container is ahead by $55,340.73; against a withdrawal rate of 32%, the Roth container is ahead by $55,340.73. Now separate the container from the product inside it. Hold the $7,000 stream, the thirty years and the 6% gross return, and change only the annual charge inside the container: a 0.05% cost leaves $548,561.04, a 1.05% cost leaves $461,098.45, and a 2.05% cost leaves $389,331.56, so the charges cost $4,846.27, $92,308.85 and $164,075.74 respectively against the gross case. An employer contribution is a separate stream that should be priced on its own: an assumed $1,800 a year of matching contributions held for thirty years at 6% becomes $142,304.74. Every figure is arithmetic under the stated assumptions, with no inflation adjustment and no state tax, and the withdrawal tax rates are illustrations.
lessons.question: Two savers put the same resources into a tax-deferred account and a Roth account, and their tax rate at contribution equals their rate at withdrawal. What is the after-tax difference?
lessons.answer: None, because paying tax before contribution and after withdrawal at the same rate produces the same after-tax result when the growth rate and horizon are the same
lessons.distractor: The Roth account wins, because growth is never taxed and therefore escapes tax on a larger amount
lessons.correction: The identity holds because the after-tax contribution in the Roth case is smaller by exactly the tax rate, and multiplication commutes: $7,000 growing to $553,407.30 and then losing 22% is $431,657.70, and $5,460 growing tax-free is also $431,657.70. The Roth does not escape tax on a larger amount; it pays the tax up front on a smaller base. The containers diverge only when the rates differ, which is why the rate at withdrawal has to be stated as an assumption before the choice means anything.

depth.definitions: A container is an account whose rules determine the timing and character of taxation; a product is what the account holds. Tax-deferred means tax is postponed until distribution. A qualified distribution is one that meets the conditions for tax-free treatment from a designated Roth account. Ordinary income is taxed at the graduated rates that apply to wages, which is how distributions from tax-deferred accounts are generally treated. A contribution limit is the maximum amount that may be contributed for a year; limits are set by statute, are adjusted periodically, and are published by the Service, which also sets out the tax on excess contributions. An employer match is an employer contribution linked to the employee's deferral, often subject to a vesting schedule that determines when the employee owns it. Required minimum distributions are mandatory withdrawals that begin at a statutory age and are calculated from a published table. Early distributions can attract an additional tax unless an exception applies, and the exceptions are statutory and vary by country. Beneficiary designations govern who receives the account and generally override a will.
depth.mechanism: The container changes the timing of tax, not the investment return, so the arithmetic compares after-tax amounts rather than balances. Because multiplication is commutative, a fixed tax rate applied before growth and the same rate applied after growth give the same result; this is why the comparison turns entirely on whether the rate now differs from the rate later, and why the honest form of the argument is a statement about the saver's income path rather than about the container. Two mechanisms make the rates differ in practice. Progressive rate schedules mean the marginal rate on a contribution today can be higher or lower than the marginal rate on a withdrawal later, depending on income in each year, and a year of unusually low income is the classic case where conversion or withdrawal enjoys a lower rate. And the container imposes its own constraints, each of which can be decisive: contribution limits cap how much of a given year's saving can be sheltered, an excess contribution is taxable, employer match may vest over time, distributions may be required from tax-deferred accounts at a statutory age, and an early withdrawal can attract an additional tax on top of income tax, which is the specific cost that makes a retirement container a poor emergency fund. The container is also not where costs hide: fees inside it, such as an expense ratio, an advisory wrap fee or a distribution fee, are charged on assets regardless of tax treatment, and the arithmetic above shows a one percentage point charge costing $92,308.85 on this thirty-year stream. Finally, every figure here is statutory or contractual in origin and therefore jurisdiction-dependent: contribution limits, the required-distribution age and the early-distribution exceptions are set by law, have changed historically, and are published annually, so they must be read from the current source rather than remembered.
depth.secondExample: Take a saver whose income is unusually low in one year, which is where the container comparison actually bites. Assume a marginal rate of 12% in that year and 22% later. Contributing $5,000 of pre-tax resources that year into a tax-deferred container costs $600 of deferred tax now and, if the whole amount is withdrawn later at 22%, $1,100 -- so the earlier, lower rate is preferable, and the same logic makes a Roth contribution unattractive in a high-rate year and attractive in a low-rate year. Now push the example to the constraint that most often decides real cases: capacity. If the saver can shelter $7,000 a year but wishes to save $12,000, the container question applies to the first $7,000 and the remaining $5,000 goes into a taxable container, where the tax treatment of dividends and realised gains is different and where the timing of sales becomes a decision. A third variant is the employer contribution: an assumed $1,800 a year of match over thirty years at 6% is $142,304.74, which is worth pricing before any contribution election, but only if the vesting schedule means the employee will actually keep it, which is a document to read rather than an assumption to make.
depth.mistake: The most common error is choosing a container on the strength of a product sold inside it, so a saver who was shown an illustration of an insurance-wrapped account concludes that the wrapper must be an efficient retirement container, when the questions that matter -- when is the money taxed, at what rate, and what does the thing inside cost -- have not been asked. The second error is believing that one container type is always right for a given age, which ignores the rate comparison that actually decides the case. The third is treating the contribution limit as a target rather than a cap. The fourth is using a retirement container as an emergency fund, which converts a temporary shock into income tax plus an additional early-distribution tax and permanently loses the shelter on the withdrawn amount. A diagnostic: state in one sentence when the money will be taxed, at what assumed rate, what the thing inside costs per year, and which statutory constraints apply -- the contribution limit for the year, the required-distribution rule, and the early-withdrawal treatment. If any of the four is unstated, the container has been chosen by habit rather than by comparison.
depth.application: Write one paragraph per container you currently use, each answering four questions: when is this money taxed, at what assumed rate, what does the investment inside cost per year as a percentage, and which statutory rules constrain it -- contribution limits, required distributions, and early-withdrawal treatment. Then compare your marginal rate now with your assumed marginal rate at withdrawal, and state which direction that comparison favours and how confident you are in the assumed future rate. Finally, list the beneficiary designation on each account and the date it was last reviewed. Self-review rubric: the record is complete when every container has all four answers, when the rate comparison is a stated number rather than a phrase, and when each cost is expressed as a percentage applied to a stated balance so its dollar effect is visible. It fails if a container is described by a product name, or if a statutory limit is quoted without the year it applies to and the source it came from.
depth.summary: A retirement account is a container that sets the timing and character of tax; the investment inside it is a separate decision. Tax-deferred and Roth containers give identical after-tax results when the rate at contribution equals the rate at withdrawal, so the choice turns on the rate comparison and on statutory capacity rather than on which container sounds more generous. Fees inside the container cost the same regardless of tax treatment, employer contributions should be priced with their vesting schedule, and contribution limits, required-distribution ages and early-withdrawal rules are statutory, jurisdiction-dependent and republished, so they must be read from the current source.

lessons.title: Capstone: a one-page plan with stated assumptions and a review date
lessons.explanation: This level has supplied the pieces: how compounding actually behaves, which lever moves a goal, how to size a reserve, how to order debts, what a credit score does and does not do, how to pose a buy-or-rent question, how inflation changes a long plan, what a payslip contains, and what a retirement container is. A capstone plan assembles them onto one page, and the page length is deliberate. A plan that cannot be written on one page usually contains either an unresolved goal or an unexamined assumption. Seven lines are enough. One: the goal, stated in dollars with its date and with the unit named, real or nominal. Two: where the money is now. Three: what is added, how often, and from which income. Four: the assumed real return, expressed as a range rather than a point. Five: the assumed inflation rate. Six: the arithmetic consequence, which is the required contribution at the middle and at the low end of the range. Seven: a review date and a falsification condition -- an observable fact that would tell you the plan is wrong. The regulator's version of the first step is the Securities and Exchange Commission's roadmap: list what you are saving for, put the most important goals first, and decide how many years you have for each, because the option must fit the time frame. Investor.gov adds the questions a plan should be able to answer, including how much is needed, how much is affordable, what your tolerance for risk is, and what you are doing to protect yourself from fraud. Everything else in a plan is decoration, and the arithmetic is what makes it auditable rather than aspirational.
lessons.example: Write the plan for a stated household. Goal: $600,000 of purchasing power in twenty-five years, so the unit is real dollars and the date is fixed. Current assets: $40,000. Contributions: $1,050 a month from salary. Assumed real return: 3.5% as the middle case, with 2% and 5% as the range. Assumed inflation: 2.5%. Arithmetic: $40,000 grows to $94,529.80 at 3.5% real, leaving $505,470.20 to be accumulated, which requires $1,056.21 a month at 3.5% real, $1,300.01 at 2% real and $848.80 at 5% real. The planned contribution of $1,050 sits just below the middle case, so the plan is close to funded and its risk is visible. Now run the review that the seventh line demands. After five years, if contributions were made as planned and the realised real return was 3.5%, the balance is $116,653.42 and the contribution needed for the remaining twenty years is $1,053.22, essentially unchanged. If the realised real return was 2% instead, the balance is $110,754.48 and the required contribution rises to $1,087.43, an increase of $34.21 a month. That is the plan's robustness: a missed return assumption by one and a half points over five years costs about thirty-four dollars a month, because a long horizon and a large contribution share dominate. Now state the goal in the other unit, which the plan requires: $600,000 of purchasing power in twenty-five years is $1,112,366.46 in nominal dollars at 2.5% inflation, and reaching that nominal figure needs $1,580.61 a month at a 6.1% nominal return but $2,163.59 at 4.0%, so a shortfall in nominal returns is not a small matter when it is compared with a fixed nominal target. Finally the falsification condition: if nominal returns deliver 6% while inflation runs at 4%, the real return is 1.9231% and the required contribution becomes about $1,392.53, a thirty-two percent increase. That single sentence is what turns a projection into a plan, because it says in advance what evidence would force a revision. All rates are assumptions for illustration; there are no fees, no taxes and no state variation in these figures, and no recommendation about any product is implied.
lessons.question: Which line of a one-page plan does the most work in preventing self-deception, and why?
lessons.answer: The falsification condition with its review date, because it states in advance what evidence would show the plan is wrong
lessons.distractor: The assumed rate of return, because a plan is only as good as the growth assumption at its centre
lessons.correction: A rate is an input and cannot check itself; a plan built on a rate with no trigger for revision simply re-asserts the assumption every year. A stated review date and a falsifiable condition convert the plan into a sequence of small, dated corrections, and they make it possible to notice a bad assumption while there is still time to change a contribution. The rate matters, but the sentence that disciplines it is the one that says what would prove it wrong.

depth.definitions: A plan is a dated document that converts preferences into arithmetic and states how it will be revised. An assumption is an input that is not known and cannot be verified in advance; a rate, an inflation figure and a future tax rate are assumptions. A goal has a date, an amount and a unit: real dollars, nominal dollars, or a different quantity such as months of expenses. A review date is a scheduled moment at which outcomes are compared with the plan. A falsification condition is an observable fact whose appearance means the plan must change. A band is a permitted range around a target before an adjustment is required. Controllable inputs are contributions, horizons, the goal and fees; uncontrollable or uncertain inputs are returns, inflation, tax rates and price growth. Monitoring is the act of observing; rebalancing is the act of correcting back to a target. A contingency is a pre-decided response to a named event, and it is cheaper to write than to improvise.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism by which a one-page plan improves outcomes is not forecasting but closure of a loop. First, writing the goal in a named unit forces the units to be consistent, which is where most plan errors are found: a real goal compared with a nominal projection, or a nominal rate applied to a real target. Second, requiring a range rather than a point turns the return assumption from a number to be defended into a range to be tested, so the plan's sensitivity is visible before a decision is made. Third, naming the controllable inputs separates the part of the plan the household can execute from the part it can only observe; contributions can be changed this month, returns cannot, and the plan should not borrow confidence from the second to justify inaction on the first. Fourth, the review date converts an otherwise unfalsifiable projection into a schedule: at each date the plan is compared with outcomes and corrected, and because a long horizon contains several reviews, an error does not have to be catastrophic to be caught. Fifth, the falsification condition prevents the specific failure mode in which a bad assumption is met with a higher assumption, which is how a projection becomes a belief. Two limits: the plan cannot include what the household has not decided, so an unresolved goal should appear as unresolved rather than be guessed; and the arithmetic is arithmetic, not advice, so a plan that ends in a recommendation about a specific product has stopped being a plan and become a sales document.
depth.secondExample: Take the same plan and stress it against two other levels, which is what the range in line four is for. If the real return is 5%, the required contribution falls to $848.80, which is $201.20 a month below the planned figure; a household that took the optimistic case as the plan would save less in the early years and would have to increase contributions later to compensate, and the later increase is larger than the earlier one because there are fewer years left. If the real return is 2%, the requirement rises to $1,300.01, which is $250.01 above the planned figure, an increase of about twenty-four percent. Compare that with the effect of a change that is entirely under the household's control: extending the horizon by five years at the 2% real rate lowers the required contribution, and increasing the contribution by $250 a month closes the gap at the middle case immediately, without any assumption changing. The comparison is the lesson's final point. The two ways to fix a plan are to change an assumption or to change an action, and only one of them can be executed.
depth.mistake: The characteristic error is a plan that is really a projection: a rate of return, a horizon and a resulting balance, with no goal unit, no range, no review date and no trigger for revision. Such a document cannot be wrong, which means it cannot be used. The second error is writing the goal in one unit and the projection in the other. The third is omitting the falsification condition, so that the first adverse result produces either panic or a raised assumption. The fourth is writing the plan for a household that does not exist, with contributions no one has agreed to. A diagnostic: show the plan to someone else and ask them to say what would have to happen for it to be wrong. If they cannot answer from the page, the missing line is the falsification condition. A second diagnostic: ask which figure in the plan can be changed this month. If the answer is none, the plan contains only assumptions.
depth.application: Write your own plan on one page with the seven lines, then have someone else read it and state, from the page alone, the goal and its unit, the three assumed inputs, the required contribution at the low and middle cases, the review date, and what would make the plan wrong. Then compute the plan's outcome under one adverse scenario and record the single change you would make in response, with the month you would make it. Self-review rubric: the plan passes when all seven lines are present, when the goal names its unit and date, when the return appears as a range with a computed contribution at the low end, and when the falsification condition is observable rather than aspirational. It fails if the goal cannot be checked against a statement, if the contribution has no owner or source, or if the only response to a bad outcome is to raise the assumed return.
depth.summary: A plan is one page of dated arithmetic: a goal in named units, current assets, contributions, a return range, an inflation assumption, the resulting required contribution, and a review date with a falsification condition. Its value comes from closing a loop rather than from forecasting, because the units are forced to be consistent, sensitivity is visible, controllable and uncontrollable inputs are separated, and errors are caught by schedule rather than by catastrophe. The test of a plan is whether someone else can say from the page what would prove it wrong, and whether any figure on it can be changed this month.

Line seven states the falsification condition: if nominal returns are 6% while inflation is 4%, the real return is 1.9231% and the required contribution becomes about $1,392.53, a 32% increase that would force a revision rather than a raised assumption.

questions.prompt: A household has the same $80,000 of capital either way. Buying a $400,000 home with it produces ownership equity of $234,028.95 after ten years under 3% appreciation and an assumed 6% selling cost; renting and investing the difference produces $231,273.51 at an assumed 5%. Ownership wins by $2,755.44. What does that margin actually tell the household?
questions.answer: That the two paths are close to a tie under those assumptions, so the decision belongs to the assumptions and to any non-financial preference, not to the arithmetic
questions.distractor: That buying is the better financial choice, because ownership produced the larger figure and the difference is positive
questions.correction: A $2,755.44 margin on a $400,000 asset is smaller than the plausible error in any single input. Move appreciation to 1% and ownership is behind by $87,219.20; move selling costs to 10% and it is behind by $18,747.22; let the renter earn 7% and it is behind by $39,543.25. A result that reverses under one assumption is a statement about the assumption, and the honest output is the table plus the sensitivity, not a verdict.

questions.prompt: A projection shows a balance of $1,000,000 in thirty years and states that a household's retirement goal is funded. The goal was written as $60,000 a year of spending in today's money. At an assumed 2.5% inflation, what has gone wrong and what is the corrected comparison?
questions.answer: The two figures are in different units; $1,000,000 in thirty years is about $476,742.69 in today's purchasing power, which has to be compared with the real goal
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because inflation reduces the value of future dollars for the household and for its spending equally, so the units cancel
questions.correction: Inflation does not cancel between a fixed nominal balance and a spending need that grows in nominal terms. The balance must be deflated to the same base date as the goal, or the goal must be inflated to the same future date: $60,000 of annual spending becomes $125,854.05 in thirty years at 2.5% inflation. Comparing $1,000,000 nominal with $60,000 real overstates the funding, which is precisely the error the units test catches.

questions.prompt: A mid-career worker receives a 3% nominal pay increase on a $5,000 monthly gross, while prices rise 2.5%. The same worker contributes $600 a month to a retirement container and is in a 22% marginal income tax bracket. Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: The raise is worth $5,024.39 in real terms, a real gain of about 0.49%, and a 6% deferral would reduce income tax but not payroll tax
questions.distractor: The raise is worth $5,150 in real terms and the deferral reduces both income tax and payroll tax, so the container is worth more than the bracket implies
questions.correction: A 3% nominal increase against 2.5% inflation is a real gain of about 0.49%, which is the difference between $5,150 of nominal pay and $5,024.39 of purchasing power. Deferrals reduce income tax; payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act are computed on wages before most deferrals, so the deferral's benefit is the marginal income tax rate applied to the deferred amount, not that rate plus payroll tax.

questions.prompt: A household holds a three-month reserve of $10,890 in cash and owes $12,000 on a card at an assumed 24%, where the monthly interest is $240. A relative says the reserve should be emptied into the card immediately because the debt costs more than the reserve earns. What is the honest comparison?
questions.answer: The certain interest saving against the cost of losing liquidity, including the expected cost of borrowing if a shock arrives while the card balance is still high
questions.distractor: The reserve's forgone return against the card's interest, which shows the card costs more and settles the question in favour of emptying the reserve
questions.correction: The card's cash cost is larger than the reserve's forgone return, which is why the comparison is uncomfortable rather than trivial. But the reserve exists to prevent borrowing at that same rate when income stops, so emptying it converts an expensive position into a more fragile one, and the expected cost depends on the probability and timing of a shock. The defensible step is to state both halves and to size the reserve against the household's actual exposure, including the access time.

questions.prompt: A plan funds a $600,000 goal from a tax-deferred retirement container. The projection shows $553,407.30 accumulated and calls the goal met. An assumed 22% tax rate will apply at withdrawal. What is the corrected finding, and what would change it?
questions.answer: The after-tax value is $431,657.70, a shortfall of $168,342.31, and a Roth container would produce the same figure if the contribution-year rate were also 22%
questions.distractor: The after-tax value is $486,998.43, a shortfall of $113,001.57, because the withdrawal rate applied to a retirement container is the lower rate
questions.correction: The container taxes the distribution, so the balance must be reduced by the rate that will apply at withdrawal; using 22% gives $431,657.70 and a shortfall of $168,342.31. The 12% figure would apply only if that were the expected rate at withdrawal. If the rate at contribution also equals the rate at withdrawal, a Roth container on the same resources produces exactly the same after-tax result, so the container choice does not repair the shortfall -- only the contribution, the horizon or the goal can.

questions.prompt: A savings brochure states that $10,000 invested at an assumed 7% a year for forty years will reach 'about $38,000', arrived at by multiplying 7% of the original by forty years. A reviewer checks the compounding and finds $149,744.58. The saver's goal was $60,000 for a specific purpose in forty years. What is the correct reading of the situation, and what single feature of the brochure's method caused the error?
questions.answer: The goal is met with $89,744.58 to spare, and the error came from adding a constant dollar amount each year instead of multiplying the whole balance including prior growth
questions.distractor: The goal is missed by $22,000, because the brochure's figure excludes the fees and taxes that a real account would charge over forty years
questions.correction: The additive method computes $700 a year for forty years and ignores the fact that each year's percentage applies to a balance that already contains earlier growth. The compounding result is $10,000 times 1.07 to the fortieth power, which is $149,744.58 before any fees or taxes. The brochure did not omit fees and a corrected additive figure would still be wrong; the method itself is the error, and its cost here is $111,744.58 of understatement.

questions.prompt: A household wants a six-month reserve of $21,780 built from monthly transfers, while carrying a $12,000 balance at an assumed 24% on which the monthly interest is $240. It can direct $500 a month to one objective or the other, or split it. After a year of putting the whole $500 into transfers, what has the reserve reached, what interest accrued on the debt, and what is the honest way to compare the two uses of the same money?
questions.answer: The reserve reaches $6,000 of the $21,780 target and the debt accrues about $2,880 of interest if untouched, so the comparison is between the certain $240 a month of avoided interest and the liquidity the reserve buys
questions.distractor: The reserve reaches $6,000 and no comparison is possible because the interest is a cost and the reserve is an asset, so the two cannot be placed on the same footing
questions.correction: They can be placed on the same footing, because both are uses of the same $500 and both have a computable consequence: paying the card saves $240 of interest in the first month, while building the reserve prevents a future month in which the household must borrow at the same rate. The target itself takes 43.6 months at $500 a month and 21.8 months at $1,000, which is why a partial reserve built first, and the interest cost stated beside it, is more defensible than either extreme asserted as a rule.

questions.prompt: A household's goal is $500,000 in twenty-five years, it currently holds nothing, and it has not decided whether the figure is nominal or real. At an assumed 2.5% inflation, what does the choice change about the required monthly contribution?
questions.answer: It changes the target from $500,000 in today's purchasing power to $926,972.05 in the dollars of the target date, with the required contribution differing accordingly at a stated real rate
questions.distractor: It changes nothing about the contribution, because inflation affects the value of the accumulated money and the goal by the same proportion over the same period
questions.correction: The two readings are different goals: $500,000 of purchasing power is $926,972.05 of nominal dollars in twenty-five years at 2.5% inflation, while $500,000 of nominal dollars is only $269,695.29 of purchasing power. In real terms the first goal requires $1,044.78 a month at an assumed 3.5% real return and the second a great deal less, so leaving the unit unstated is a mistake worth hundreds of dollars a month.

questions.prompt: A card carries $3,000 against a $6,000 limit. The holder pays down $1,500 and holds the rest, and separately receives a paid offer to 'improve' the account's profile. Which changes are computable facts, and which are unverifiable claims?
questions.answer: Utilisation moves from 50.0% to 25.0% and the interest saved is computable; any claim about a specific number of score points is unverifiable because models and versions differ and their weights are not published computeably
questions.distractor: Utilisation moves from 50.0% to 25.0% and a lower utilisation raises the score by a knowable amount once the reporting company's model is named
questions.correction: The utilisation change is arithmetic and the interest saving follows from the rate, but the point impact of any change depends on the model, its version and the rest of the file, and no published weighting permits computing it. The Bureau's guidance describes directions, not magnitudes, and states that carrying a balance is not required. A claim that names a model still cannot convert a utilisation change into points, so the honest defence of the paydown is the interest saved, not a promised score.

questions.prompt: A household is choosing between two mortgage-rate outcomes on an assumed $300,000 thirty-year loan: 6.5%, costing $1,896.20 a month and $382,633.47 of interest, against 6.0%, costing $1,798.65 and $347,514.57. In the same month, a ten-year buy-or-rent comparison under stated assumptions puts ownership ahead by only $2,755.44. What does placing the two numbers side by side show?
questions.answer: The $35,118.90 lifetime difference in borrowing cost is more than twelve times the entire ten-year ownership margin, so the price of credit can outweigh the tenure question
questions.distractor: The two numbers are unrelated, because one concerns borrowing cost and the other concerns tenure, and combining them double-counts the effect of rates
questions.correction: They are related through the same interest rate, which enters both the ownership cost and the price of credit. The margin of $2,755.44 is the net result of many assumptions including the rate, while $35,118.90 is a direct consequence of half a percentage point. The exercise is not to add them but to rank the sensitivities: the rate assumption in the comparison is large enough to dominate the result, which is why the comparison must be re-run with each plausible rate rather than reported once.

questions.prompt: A household is deciding whether to buy or to keep renting, and has run the ten-year comparison. Its expected tenure is uncertain: there is a chance it moves in three years. Under the stated assumptions, ownership is behind at year two by $24,184.40, behind at year five by $19,962.87, behind at year eight by $9,060.16, ahead at year ten by $2,755.44 and ahead at year fifteen by $52,696.20. What should the household do with that information?
questions.answer: Treat the horizon as the decisive input, note that early exit is dominated by transaction costs and interest, and price the cost of a mistaken move before deciding
questions.distractor: Choose ownership anyway, because the comparison is favourable in the long run and a three-year move is a low-probability event that can be ignored
questions.correction: The progression shows that the answer changes sign with the horizon, so a household whose tenure is uncertain is exposed to the losing years even if it intends to stay. The 6% selling cost on the ten-year value alone is $32,253.99, which is larger than every margin in the series up to year ten. The correct use of the numbers is to state the tenure assumption, run the case for the shortest plausible stay, and treat the probability of moving as part of the decision rather than as a footnote.

questions.prompt: A worker earns $5,000 a month and receives a 3% nominal increase while inflation runs at 2.5%. The employer's withholding is computed on the new nominal pay. What is the real value of the increase, and what does the withholding arrangement imply about the relationship between tax and inflation?
questions.answer: The increase is worth $5,024.39 in real terms, a real gain of about 0.49%, while withholding and any income tax computed on the nominal amount take a share of the whole nominal increase
questions.distractor: The increase is worth $5,150 in real terms, because withholding is computed after adjusting wages for inflation by the annual adjustment to the standard deduction
questions.correction: Nominal pay of $5,150 is worth $5,024.39 in purchasing power at 2.5% inflation, so the real gain is 0.49%, not 3%. Tax is levied on nominal amounts and the standard deduction and brackets are adjusted annually by statute, which reduces but does not eliminate the effect: an inflation adjustment to the brackets moves the boundaries, whereas the raise itself is taxed at the marginal rate on the nominal increase. The two adjustments are different mechanisms and should not be treated as cancelling.

questions.prompt: A worker defers 6% of a $5,000 monthly gross into an employer plan, which is $300 a month, and is in an assumed 22% marginal income tax bracket. Payroll taxes are $382.50 a month, unchanged. After thirty years at an assumed 6% annual return, what has the deferral stream become, and what did the election fail to reduce?
questions.answer: An annual deposit of $3,600 for thirty years at 6% becomes $284,609.47, and the election did not reduce payroll taxes, which are computed on wages before most deferrals
questions.distractor: An annual deposit of $3,600 for thirty years at 6% becomes $284,609.47, and the election reduced both income tax and payroll taxes by the marginal rate
questions.correction: The deferral reduces taxable income, so the income tax benefit is the marginal rate applied to the deferred amount, which is 22% of $3,600, or $792 a year in the illustration. Payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act are computed on wages before most deferrals, so the $382.50 is unaffected. The stream's future value is arithmetic on the stated contribution, rate and horizon, with no inflation adjustment and no fees.

questions.prompt: A household with a three-month reserve of $10,890 faces a $10,000 emergency. Withdrawing from a retirement container would cost an assumed 22% in income tax plus an assumed 10% early-distribution tax. It could also rebuild the reserve instead. What is the arithmetic comparison?
questions.answer: The withdrawal costs about $3,200 on $10,000, whereas the reserve's annual opportunity cost in the stated illustration was about $130.68, which is the reason a small reserve is cheap insurance against a taxable withdrawal
questions.distractor: The withdrawal costs about $2,200 on $10,000, since the early-distribution tax replaces the income tax rather than being charged in addition to it
questions.correction: The early-distribution tax is charged in addition to the income tax that applies to the distribution, so the illustration costs $2,200 plus $1,000, which is $3,200. Set beside the reserve's stated annual opportunity cost of about $130.68, the comparison shows that roughly twenty-four years of holding costs equal one avoided withdrawal event. Exceptions to the additional tax exist and the rules are statutory and jurisdiction-dependent, so the applicable treatment must be checked in the current source before relying on any figure.

questions.prompt: A saver can commit $7,000 a year of pre-tax resources for thirty years at an assumed 6% return. Her marginal rate this year is 12%. She expects the rate at withdrawal to be 32%. A colleague says the choice between a tax-deferred container and a Roth container does not matter because the rates are just timing. What does the arithmetic show?
questions.answer: The Roth wins here: contributing after tax at 12% gives $486,998.43 tax-free, against $376,316.97 after tax from the tax-deferred container at a 32% withdrawal rate
questions.distractor: The tax-deferred container wins here: it accumulates $553,407.30 and the deferral always beats paying tax early, whatever the later rate
questions.correction: The container comparison depends entirely on the two rates. At a 12% rate at contribution, $7,000 of pre-tax resources becomes $6,160 contributed, which grows tax-free to $486,998.43. The tax-deferred container grows $7,000 a year to $553,407.30 and then loses 32% at withdrawal, leaving $376,316.97. The difference of $110,681.46 is produced by the rate gap, not by the container's name, and if the rates were equal the two results would be identical.

questions.prompt: A household treats a $600 monthly contribution as '12% of income' because gross pay is $5,000 a month. After payroll taxes of $382.50 and illustrative federal withholding of $418.33, net pay is $4,199.17. What is the correct statement of the saving rate, and what does the difference reveal about a plan built on gross income?
questions.answer: The contribution is 12.0% of gross and 14.29% of net, so a plan written on gross income understates the share of take-home pay that must be committed
questions.distractor: The contribution is 14.29% of gross and 12.0% of net, so the plan written on gross income understates the burden
questions.correction: Net pay is smaller than gross, so the same dollar contribution is a larger share of net: $600 is 12.0% of $5,000 and 14.29% of $4,199.17. A plan that states its saving rate against gross income while the money must come out of net pay will feel harder to sustain than its arithmetic suggests, and the denominator should be stated alongside every saving-rate figure. The withholding figure depends on elections and on the year's published parameters, so it should be verified against a payslip.

questions.prompt: A one-page plan states: contribute $600 a month, assume 9% a year, and reach $500,000 in twenty-five years. It holds no reserve, carries a $12,000 balance at an assumed 24%, and names no review date. Under an assumed 5% return the contributions produce $357,305.83, and reaching $500,000 on $600 a month would need about 7.18% a year. Which finding should be reported first, and why?
questions.answer: The plan fails on its own terms even if nothing goes wrong: the return assumption is doing the work, and the debt alone consumes $2,880 a year against $7,200 of contributions
questions.distractor: The missing reserve is the first finding, because no plan can be evaluated until a shock is modelled and every other figure depends on it
questions.correction: Both findings are real, but the decisive one is that the plan's arithmetic only closes if an assumption holds for twenty-five consecutive years, which no plan can verify in advance. The debt's $240 of monthly interest is $2,880 a year against $7,200 of contributions, which competes directly with the goal, and the correctly required contribution at 5% is $839.62 rather than $600. A reserve matters because it prevents borrowing at that rate, but reporting it first would leave the plan's own arithmetic unexamined.
